message.content:
**“Largest” — what does it mean?**

| Term | Typical definition |
|------|--------------------|
| **Planet** | A body whose mass is below ≈ 13 M<sub>J</sub>, i.e. too low to ignite deuterium fusion. |
| **Brown‑dwarf / “failed star”** | Mass above ≈ 13 M<sub>J</sub>; can fuse deuterium briefly. |

Because the boundary is set by *mass*, the term “largest planet” usually refers either to:
* the greatest **size (radius)** found for a bona‑fide planet (< 13 MJ);  
* or, when people speak loosely, the biggest **object orbiting another star**, even if it sits just over the deuterium‑fusion threshold.

Below you’ll see both perspectives.

---

### 1️⃣ Biggest **planetary‐mass** bodies (≤ ≈ 13 MJ)

These are all still classified as planets according to the modern convention. Their sizes tend to cluster near Jupiter’s radius, but many become noticeably puffier (“inflated”) when they’re very close to their parent star.

| Planet | Host Star | Distance (AU) | Mass (M<sub>J</sub>) | Radius (R<sub>J</sub>) | Notes |
|--------|-----------|---------------|---------------------|-----------------------|-------|
| **WASP‑17b** | F6V | 0.025 | 0.49 | **1.99 ± 0.04** | One of the flattest/most bloated hot Jupiters ever seen. |
| **HAT‑P‑32b** | G0V | 0.034 | 0.86 | 1.78 | Extremely low density – almost a “puffy ball.” |
| **Kepler‑75b** | G-type | 0.045 | 0.95 | 1.73 | Very short orbital period (∼ 1 day). |
| **HD 209458b** | Sun‑like | 0.047 | 0.69 | 1.38 | First transiting exoplanet detected; classic hot Jupiter. |
| **KELT‑9b** | A0V | 0.048 | 2.88 | 1.64 | Ultra‑hot; atmosphere partially ionized. |

**Key point:** Even the most inflated hot Jupiters barely double Jupiter’s radius. Gravitational compression keeps the bulk of such planets within roughly 2 × R<sub>J</sub>. Beyond this, the material cannot support further expansion without breaking apart.

---

### 2️⃣ Directly imaged giant planets & borderline brown dwarfs

When astronomers look farther out (tens–hundreds of AU) they often discover companions that sit right on the edge of the planet/brown‑dwarf divide. These objects typically have masses ranging from ∼ 5 to 30 M<sub>J</sub> and radii comparable to Jupiter’s (because once you hit the deuterium‑burning regime, additional mass mainly adds gravity rather than volume).

| Object | System | Separation (AU) | Mass (M<sub>J</sub>) | Approximate Radius | Classification |
|--------|--------|-----------------|---------------------|-------------------|----------------|
| **HR 8799 b,c,d,e** | A0V | 15–70 | 5–10 | ≃ 1 R<sub>J</sub> | Planets (just under 13 MJ) |
| **β Pic b** | A6V | 9 | 9.8 | ≃ 1.2 R<sub>J</sub> | Planet |
| **GQ Lupi b** | T Tauri | 68 | 14 | ≃ 1.5 R<sub>J</sub> | Borderline brown dwarf |
| **HD 106906 b** | A2V | 650 | 11 | ≃ 1.2 R<sub>J</sub> | Planet (wide separation) |
| **PSO J318.5338−22.8603** | Free‑floating | — | 8.5 | ≃ 1.3 R<sub>J</sub> | Isolated planetary‑mass object |

Even here, the physical radius rarely exceeds ~1.5 R<sub>J</sub> despite higher masses. This reflects how self‑gravity compresses matter into a relatively compact sphere.

---

### 3️⃣ What do we really know about the “biggest” thing in the cosmos?

* **Observations are limited by distance and brightness.** Most exoplanets are inferred via indirect methods (transits, radial velocity, microlensing). Only a handful are bright enough for detailed atmospheric studies or direct imaging.
* **Mass limits are clearer than radius limits.** Because mass determines whether deuterium burning occurs, the community uses it as the primary classification metric. Radii saturate quickly due to gravitational equilibrium.
* **Future surveys (Roman Space Telescope, JWST follow‑ups, ELTs) will push detection thresholds lower/higher, potentially finding truly gigantic gaseous worlds (> 20 RJ?) or confirming that nature simply doesn’t produce stable spheres much larger than a few Jupiter radii.**

In summary:

| Category | Current Record (Radius) | Current Record (Mass) |
|----------|-------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Planets ≤ 13 MJ** | ~1.99 R<sub>J</sub> (WASP‑17b) | ~13 MJ (upper bound) |
| **Directly Imaged Giants/Brown Dwarfs** | ~1.5 R<sub>J</sub> (typical) | Up to ~30 MJ (rare) |

So while we’ve identified several “giant” planets that dwarf Earth and Mars, none yet surpasses roughly twice Jupiter’s radius. If anything larger exists, it remains hidden behind observational challenges—or perhaps physics itself forbids stable bodies significantly exceeding that scale.
